arxiv:2610.41965.text: Microswimmers lose by swimming selfishly. From Albert Alonso. At low Reynolds number, swimmers affect one another through the flows they create, so a swimmer's best motion can depend on its neighbors. Using a computer model to optimize soft swimmers' shape changes, the study finds that a lone swimmer settles into a traveling wave. In a pair, selfish swimmers adjust too little to their neighbors and end up worse off than if they kept their solo motions. Swimmers that value a neighbor's progress can recover the missed gain, showing how hydrodynamics can turn swimming together into a social dilemma.

arxiv:2610.41103.text: Optimal climate policy in incomplete electricity markets. From Emil Dimanchev and colleagues. Incomplete electricity contracts can leave investors and consumers exposed to price swings, raising questions about how climate policy should respond. A game-theoretic model examines policy choices when gas prices and demand are uncertain and market participants react to policy. In illustrative experiments, renewable subsidies and carbon prices also insure consumers by encouraging renewable investment, so incomplete markets call for higher levels of both. Subsidies provide stronger insurance, and in some cases become more economically efficient than carbon pricing.

arxiv:2610.40942.text: Immersed Boundary Electrodiffusion in the Wasserstein Gradient Flow Formalism: Global Well-Posedness, Non-Equilibrium Thermodynamics, and Singular Asymptotics. From Pilhwa Lee. The work addresses how to describe ion transport across membranes when diffusion, electric forces, and energy-driven pumps act together. It builds an optimal transport framework that treats passive motion as downhill movement in free energy and represents active pumps as additional forces. The framework establishes global weak solutions and an energy balance, and shows that steady states are stable when a curvature condition holds. It also connects smoothed membrane models to sharp interfaces and explains how thin electric boundary layers lead to electrically neutral bulk regions.

arxiv:2610.42042.text: A richness-sensitive Acoustic Biodiversity Index from species-level detections: classifier benchmarking, false-positive control and validation against standard soundscape indices in an African savanna and an urban zoo. From Muhammad Saeed and colleagues. Acoustic indices often measure sound energy rather than the species making it, so they can miss changes in species richness. This study builds an Acoustic Biodiversity Index from species detections, benchmarks detection methods, and checks false positives and recording effort. Across a Zimbabwean savanna and three zoo habitats, the index closely tracked species richness, while six standard sound indices did not track it as well. The results show why species-level checks and a clear regional reference pool matter.

arxiv:2610.41447.text: Why delivered costs understate prices in an integrated global hydrogen market. From Bastian Weißenburger and colleagues. Delivered costs are often used to predict hydrogen import prices, but they measure average supply costs, not the value of one more unit in a connected market. An eighty-one-region model compares costs and prices with demand in one region and with demand worldwide. In 2045, prices exceed costs in seventy-eight regions, by an average of sixty-three euros per megawatt-hour on a demand-weighted basis. Most of that gap comes from market prices differing from the average cost of delivered supply, so low-cost imports do not guarantee low regional prices.

arxiv:2610.40948.text: Temporal and spatial couplings in the dynamics of human walking and running. From Mustafa Mert Ankarali. Models of walking and running often assume that each step depends only on the last, and that motion in two directions can be studied separately. Across seven datasets from seventy-one people, step-to-step models showed that looking back two steps could reduce prediction error by up to twenty-nine percent. But most of that apparent memory disappeared when the models allowed the gait pattern to drift slowly and accounted for measurement noise. Running retained more memory than walking, while coupling between motion in the two planes was present but weak.

arxiv:2610.40867.text: GraphTFactor: A graph-based approach for proteins transcription factor prediction. From Domenico Amato and colleagues. Identifying transcription factors, which regulate gene expression, is an important task in computational biology. GraphTFactor turns protein sequences into graphs and uses them to classify transcription factors, handling sequences of different lengths while retaining relationships between their parts. On benchmark datasets, it outperforms existing methods and highlights sequence regions that contribute to its predictions. The team also provides software and an interactive web app for predicting transcription factors from custom sequences.

arxiv:2610.42126.text: Physiological Trajectories and Observation Patterns in ICU Mortality Prediction: Transportability Under Changing Measurement Conditions. From Benjamin T. Pike. Predicting death in intensive care units across hospitals is difficult when both patients and measurement practices differ. This study compared models using recent readings, trends over time, and patterns in how often and when measurements were taken. Trends improved prediction when models moved to another hospital network, while measurement patterns did not transfer clearly. Their value also depended on having measurements spread across the prediction window, showing that models should be tested under changing measurement conditions.

arxiv:2610.41963.text: Zero Crossings on the Accuracy-Smoothness Frontier: Maximal Monotone and Minimal Inflection Non Stationary Predictors. From Marc Wildi. Non-stationary forecasts face a trade-off between accuracy and smoothness, but existing smoothness measures are designed for stationary data. This work extends the Smooth Sign Accuracy framework to integrated processes, choosing predictors that control how often the forecast changes direction or bends. It derives an efficient accuracy-smoothness frontier and a trend measure that controls these changes without imposing an artificial structure on the data. The method has a global optimum in its feasible region, and its finite-sample solutions converge to an asymptotic predictor.

arxiv:2610.41930.text: Nonequilibrium Transient Centers in Continuous-Time Systems. From Anthony Pasion and colleagues. Many ecological and epidemic systems can change very slowly for a long time, then shift quickly, making short-term behavior more useful than the eventual outcome. This work introduces nonequilibrium transient centers, where an observable stays nearly constant even though the system as a whole is not at equilibrium. It develops criteria for when nearby trajectories remain in this slow regime and when they escape. In a delayed epidemic model, the framework explains how infection can stay near zero before resurging.

arxiv:2610.41798.text: A two-stage diffusion-driven morphogenesis model with evolving connectivity. From Alexander Safonov. Diatom shells form when separate silica ribs branch and then join, but earlier models captured only one of these steps. This model uses diffusion on a fixed mesh to represent both stages: strong local flux first drives branching growth, then suppresses growth to leave pores between the ribs. Changing the thresholds produces distinct patterns in each stage. In a reference run, the pores are regularly spaced and absent near the edges, matching observed diatom valves.

arxiv:2610.41736.text: Locality-Controlled Out-of-Distribution Guidance for Robust Regulatory DNA Sequence Design. From Dabin Jeong and colleagues. Designing regulatory DNA that drives a desired level of gene activity is difficult: methods can raise predicted activity by producing sequences that are unrealistic or too similar to known examples. LOCOGEN guides a sequence-generation model differently across positions, protecting important motif locations while allowing more exploration in background regions. It works during generation without retraining the model. Across three cell types, it achieves high activity, novelty, and plausibility together, a combination that existing comparison methods did not reach.

arxiv:2610.41725.text: An extension of the classic Buneman theorem from phylogenetic trees to networks. From Mirko Wilde and colleagues. Parsimony can reveal the structure of evolutionary trees, but it is less clear what it can identify in networks that include events like hybridization. This work develops a framework for testing which network features can be recovered from character data under hardwired parsimony. It shows that a network's tree of blobs can be reconstructed from its simplest alignment, extending a classic result for trees. But cycles of length five or more cannot always be uniquely identified from the data.

arxiv:2610.41684.text: Hyperbolic embedding of higher-order simplicial networks. From Martin Guillemaud and colleagues. Many networks involve groups interacting together, but pairwise maps cannot tell a shared group interaction from separate links between the same nodes. The hyperbolic higher-order embedding places groups and their interactions in a curved map, where the area of a triangle reflects how compactly a group is represented. Tests on simulated and real networks found that group interactions formed smaller triangles and that the method recovered node groups more accurately than pairwise approaches. Its group-recovery performance was competitive with Euclidean maps.

arxiv:2610.41650.text: Genetic weight of a mutant in a biparental Moran model with infinite selection. From Camille Coron and colleagues. The work asks how much genetic weight a single strongly advantageous mutant contributes as it spreads through a population with biparental reproduction and infinite selection. It proves that the contributions in advantaged and disadvantaged subgroups follow a shared deterministic profile, multiplied by a random amplitude. That randomness arises during the mutant's earliest growth and is carried forward as the population changes. An eigenmode martingale captures the imbalance that sets the amplitude, which is also characterized by a smoothing equation.

arxiv:2610.41634.text: CosquaredODE: Conditionally Coarse-Grained Model Discovery for Rewiring in Biochemical Networks. From Theodore de Pomereu and colleagues. Biochemical networks can change their effective signaling routes with cellular context, but sparse, correlated measurements make it hard to learn a full network model. Co-squared ODE focuses on the parts that change, using a conditional mask to select markers and a compressed learned term to represent the rest. On single-cell data covering thirty cancer-related overexpressions, it reduced a thirty-marker panel to ten state variables while matching the predictive accuracy of a full-panel model. Different marker choices fit equally well, suggesting the data cannot by themselves reveal the underlying biology.

arxiv:2610.41361.text: Identification through Heteroskedasticity in One Lemma: Partial Identification, an Eigenvalue Construction, and a Caution on Rank Tests. From George Milunovich. Identifying shocks from changing volatility can fail when different shocks follow the same pattern of variance over time. This teaching note brings results from several volatility models together in one lemma, proved with a short linear algebra argument. It shows that shocks with distinct variance paths are identified up to sign and labelling, while shocks sharing a path are identifiable only up to rotation. A generalised eigenvalue problem recovers the structural coefficients, and the note warns that rank tests count independent variance paths, not identified shocks.

arxiv:2610.41109.text: Transmission and filtering of stochastic rhythms in bursty gene expression. From Chen Jia. Cells must decide which rhythmic regulatory signals to preserve in gene expression, but the roles of degradation, bursting, and variation in signal timing have been hard to explain together. This work develops a mathematical framework that predicts how those factors shape rhythms in downstream genes, even when upstream signals have complex dynamics and memory. It finds that more frequent bursts and stronger signal modulation favor rhythm transmission, while irregular timing weakens it; larger bursts do not change transmission efficiency. A predicted degradation threshold also separates all ten p53 target proteins known to pulse from those that do not.

arxiv:2610.41070.text: D2ML: Models for Direct-to-Biology Small Molecule Screening. From AkshatKumar Nigam and colleagues. Direct-to-biology screening tests newly made molecules without purification, but uncertain concentrations can make the results hard to use for machine learning. Assay-aware models account for the different stages of screening, and a joint model that shares information across them improved predictions over separate models. Its biggest gain was in predicting selectivity from crude dose-response tests. Models also guided the selection of new compounds, yielding one with stronger ROS1 potency and greater selectivity over TRKB than the most selective compound in the training data.

arxiv:2610.41046.text: Localizing predictive concepts encoded in neural representations via hierarchical testing. From Viktoriia Huryn and colleagues. Deep learning models can learn DNA motifs that help predict gene activity, but it is hard to tell which internal units matter without risking false discoveries. CUTTIE groups units into a hierarchy and tests those groups from broad to specific, controlling the chance of false findings across the search. In simulation, it finds the groups whose concepts affect the prediction. Applied to a model of chromatin accessibility, it identifies groups linked to known regulatory motifs.

arxiv:2610.41284.text: Deterministic Implementation of Mean-Preserving Contractions. From Junze Sun. The work asks whether a designer needs random signals to produce a chosen distribution of posterior means. It shows that for an atomless prior with a finite first moment, every mean-preserving contraction can be implemented deterministically. So when objectives and constraints depend only on posterior means, allowing randomization does not improve the designer's value. The work also gives a constructive method and applies the result to pricing and robust persuasion.

arxiv:2610.41029.text: Contribution of chromosome-naïve transposon-seeded network of DNA templates to intracellular pools of protein dimers of liquid-liquid phase-separated condensate-forming proteins. From Gennadi Glinsky. How cells build membraneless protein condensates, and how that process connects to other protein complexes, is still not well understood. This study links condensate-forming proteins to chains of protein interactions involved in assembling multiprotein complexes, while finding no condensate-negative proteins in those chains. Its analysis supports a model in which transposon-seeded DNA templates help start these interaction chains, enabling condensates and structured complexes to assemble in parallel. It also identifies protein changes at dimer interfaces and suggests many protein pairs for further study.

arxiv:2610.40839.text: Expression of White and Gray Matter Autism Functional Network Connectivity Signatures in Infancy. From Qiang Li and colleagues. Autism connectivity studies often examine gray matter or white matter separately, leaving their interactions and development less understood. This study combined signals from both tissue types and measured autism-related connectivity patterns in existing autism data and an independent infant group. It found reduced connections centered on the paralimbic network and stronger connections between white and gray matter centered on the frontal network. Infants with higher familial likelihood of autism showed greater expression of these patterns, but the findings do not predict individual diagnoses.

arxiv:2610.40894.text: Basis statistics for phylogenetic tree shape: tree balance formulas beyond expectations. From Daniel J. Bauman and colleagues. Comparing tree balance measures is difficult because rooted, binary evolutionary trees form an enormous space. This work maps tree shapes into smaller sets of basis statistics, where many balance measures become linear combinations. Under the Yule–Harding model, the framework gives exact means for seventeen indices, including nine whose means were not previously available. It also calculates exact variances for all seventeen and covariance and correlation for every pair, helping researchers study how different measures relate.

arxiv:2610.42052.text: Valid GMM Inference with Non-parametrically Generated Discrete Type. From Taegyu Yang. Researchers often infer unobserved economic categories from data, but errors in that first prediction step can bias later estimates. This work smooths the sharp category boundaries, then builds a bias-corrected method for generalized method of moments estimation. Under regularity conditions, the estimates are consistent at the square root of the sample size times the smoothing parameter rate and have an asymptotically normal distribution. That slower rate reflects the cost of correcting bias when predicted categories enter the estimation in a discontinuous way.
